title: Bioenergetics
explain: This lecture studies how cells obtain, transfer, and spend energy through chemical reactions.
mustKnow: Bioenergetics connects cellular chemistry with energy flow.

terms.meaning: Study of energy changes and transfers in living systems.

title: Bioenergetics reference
explain: This is a source-link slide and introduces no additional examinable concept.
mustKnow: The lecture topic remains bioenergetics.

title: What metabolism accomplishes
explain: Metabolism is the coordinated reaction network that captures energy, converts nutrients into cellular building blocks, joins small units into macromolecules, and makes or removes specialized molecules.
mustKnow: Cells obtain energy from sunlight or energy-rich nutrients.
Nutrients are converted into cellular precursors.
Monomers are polymerized into proteins, nucleic acids, and polysaccharides.
Metabolism also handles lipids, messengers, and pigments.

terms.meaning: Starting molecule used to build another molecule.
Large cellular molecule built from smaller units.

interaction.q: Which is a function of metabolism shown on this slide?
interaction.explanation: Metabolism includes obtaining chemical energy by capturing sunlight or degrading energy-rich nutrients.

title: Nitrogen and unavoidable energy loss
explain: Organisms need nitrogen to build amino acids and nucleic acids. During metabolism, not all energy remains useful: some becomes heat and entropy increases.
mustKnow: Nitrogen is required for amino-acid and nucleic-acid synthesis.
Metabolic energy conversion loses some useful free energy as heat.
Entropy inevitably increases.

terms.meaning: Energy available to perform useful work.
Measure associated with energy dispersal or disorder.

interaction.q: What happens inevitably during metabolic energy conversion?
options: Nitrogen is converted entirely to ATP
interaction.explanation: The slide states that useful free energy is lost and unusable energy, heat and entropy, increases.

title: Definition of metabolism
explain: Metabolism is the complete set of chemical transformations in a cell or organism. These transformations occur as ordered, enzyme-catalyzed metabolic pathways.
mustKnow: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical transformations.
Metabolic pathways are series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions.

terms.meaning: Ordered series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions.

interaction.q: Which best defines metabolism?
options: All chemical transformations in a cell or organism
interaction.explanation: The slide defines metabolism as the sum of all chemical transformations in a cell or organism.

title: Catabolic and anabolic pathway patterns
explain: Catabolism usually funnels many starting molecules toward fewer products, so it is convergent. Anabolism starts from a smaller set of precursors and builds many products, so it is divergent. Separate enzymes prevent a futile back-and-forth cycle.
mustKnow: Catabolic pathways are generally convergent.
Anabolic pathways are generally divergent.
Anabolism and catabolism use separate enzyme sets.
Pathways may be linear, branched, or cyclic.

terms.meaning: Breakdown pathways that extract energy from nutrients.
Biosynthetic pathways that use energy to make cellular molecules.
Several inputs lead toward a common product.
One precursor leads toward several products.

interaction.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Both always use the same enzymes
interaction.explanation: The slide explicitly identifies catabolic pathways as convergent and anabolic pathways as divergent.

title: Reciprocal regulation and compartmentation
explain: Opposing anabolic and catabolic routes are controlled reciprocally, may follow different reaction sequences, and can occur in different cellular compartments. This prevents both directions from running strongly at once.
mustKnow: Opposing pathways are reciprocally regulated.
Opposite pathways may use different reaction sequences.
Paired pathways can occur in different compartments.

terms.meaning: Activation of one opposing pathway is coordinated with inhibition of the other.
Separation of processes into different cellular locations.

interaction.label: Opposing pathways are separated and reciprocally controlled

title: Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics
explain: As substrate concentration rises, reaction rate approaches a maximum because the enzyme becomes saturated. Vmax is that maximum rate; KM is the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax.
mustKnow: Vmax is reached near saturating substrate concentration.
At substrate concentration KM, rate equals Vmax/2.
Vmax applies for a given enzyme concentration.

terms.meaning: Maximum reaction rate at enzyme saturation.
Substrate concentration at which rate is half Vmax.
Condition in which adding substrate produces little further rate increase.

interaction.q: When [S] equals KM, the reaction rate is:
interaction.explanation: KM is numerically equal to the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax.

title: Regulation of metabolism
explain: The slide lists three ways metabolism is controlled: substrate availability, allosteric regulation, and hormonal regulation. Each changes whether an enzyme can efficiently run its reaction.
mustKnow: Low substrate relative to KM limits reaction rate.
Allosteric molecules bind enzymes and alter activity.
Hormones can change enzyme synthesis or degradation.

terms.meaning: Control by a molecule binding away from the active site and changing enzyme activity.
Control of metabolism in response to hormones.

interaction.q: Which is NOT one of the regulatory mechanisms listed?
interaction.explanation: The slide lists substrate availability, allosteric regulation, and hormonal regulation.

title: Thermodynamic quantities
explain: ΔG combines the effects of enthalpy and entropy and predicts energetic favorability. Negative ΔG means energy release; positive ΔG means energy input is required. ΔH tracks heat change, while ΔS tracks entropy change.
mustKnow: Negative ΔG describes an exergonic reaction.
Positive ΔG describes an endergonic reaction.
Negative ΔH releases heat; positive ΔH absorbs heat.
Positive ΔS means products are more disordered than reactants.

terms.meaning: Free-energy change of a reaction.
Enthalpy or heat change.
Entropy change.
Energy-releasing reaction with negative ΔG.

interaction.q: A reaction with positive ΔG is:
interaction.explanation: The slide states that positive ΔG means the reaction requires energy and is endergonic.

title: Relationship among ΔG, ΔH, and ΔS
explain: The equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS combines heat and entropy effects at temperature T. A reaction is favorable when ΔG is negative; heat release or increased entropy tends to make ΔG more negative.
mustKnow: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
A negative ΔG indicates a favorable reaction.
Negative ΔH and positive ΔS favor a negative ΔG.

terms.meaning: Reaction with negative free-energy change under the stated conditions.
Absolute temperature used in the free-energy equation.

interaction.q: Which combination most favors a negative ΔG?
interaction.explanation: Heat release gives negative ΔH and increasing entropy gives positive ΔS; both lower ΔG.

title: Biochemical standard state and reaction quotient
explain: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant uses product concentrations over reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient. Biochemical standard conditions set pH 7 and treat water as 55.5 M; away from equilibrium, ΔG supplies the driving force.
mustKnow: Keq = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b.
Biochemical standard state uses [H+] = 10^-7 M, or pH 7.
Water is treated as 55.5 M.
When not at equilibrium, ΔG drives movement toward equilibrium.

terms.meaning: Concentration ratio describing a reaction at equilibrium.
Standard convention using pH 7 for biochemical reactions.

interaction.q: What pH is used in the biochemical standard state?
interaction.explanation: The slide defines [H+] as 10^-7 M, which is pH 7.

title: Exergonic reactions
explain: An exergonic reaction releases free energy, has negative ΔG, and can perform work. It may occur spontaneously under the given conditions, although that does not say how fast it occurs.
mustKnow: Exergonic reactions release energy.
Exergonic reactions have ΔG < 0.
They can perform work and include many catabolic reactions.
Exergonic does not mean instantaneous.

terms.meaning: Reaction with negative ΔG that releases free energy.
Thermodynamically able to proceed without net energy input under stated conditions.

interaction.q: Which statement describes an exergonic reaction?
interaction.explanation: Exergonic reactions release free energy and have negative ΔG.

title: Endergonic reactions
explain: An endergonic reaction requires energy input and has positive ΔG. Many anabolic reactions are endergonic. If the reaction is reversed, the reverse direction is exergonic.
mustKnow: Endergonic reactions require energy input.
Endergonic reactions have ΔG > 0.
Many anabolic reactions are endergonic.
The reverse of an endergonic reaction is exergonic.

terms.meaning: Reaction with positive ΔG that requires free-energy input.
Reaction involved in building complex cellular molecules.

interaction.q: Most anabolic reactions are described on this slide as:
interaction.explanation: The slide states that most anabolic reactions are endergonic in nature.

title: Standard free energy and equilibrium
explain: Standard transformed free energy is linked to the equilibrium constant by ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq. A large equilibrium constant gives a negative ΔG°′ and favors products under standard biochemical conditions.
mustKnow: ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq.
K′eq > 1 corresponds to negative ΔG°′.
K′eq = 1 corresponds to ΔG°′ = 0.
K′eq < 1 corresponds to positive ΔG°′.

terms.meaning: Standard transformed free-energy change at biochemical standard conditions.
Equilibrium constant using biochemical conventions.

interaction.q: If K′eq is greater than 1, ΔG°′ is:
interaction.explanation: Because ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq, K′eq greater than 1 gives a negative value.

title: Energy-unit conversion
explain: Biochemical energies may be written in kilocalories or kilojoules. Convert using 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.
mustKnow: 1 kcal equals 4.184 kJ.

terms.meaning: Kilocalorie, a unit of energy.
Kilojoule, a unit of energy.

interaction.q: 1 kcal is equal to:
interaction.explanation: The conversion displayed is 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.

title: Calculating ΔG°′ from K′eq
explain: For A ⇌ B with K′eq = 12, inserting the value into ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq gives about −6.15 kJ/mol. The negative sign means the standard-condition reaction favors B.
mustKnow: A K′eq of 12 gives negative ΔG°′.
The shown result is approximately −6.15 kJ/mol.
Negative ΔG°′ favors the forward direction under standard conditions.

terms.meaning: Gas constant used in thermodynamic equations.
Natural logarithm.

interaction.q: For A ⇌ B with K′eq = 12, what sign does ΔG°′ have?
interaction.explanation: The calculation on the slide gives approximately −6.15 kJ/mol.

title: Actual free-energy change
explain: Actual ΔG depends on both the reaction's standard ΔG°′ and the current product-to-reactant concentration ratio. Changing concentrations can therefore change the direction favored inside a cell.
mustKnow: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([C][D]/[A][B]) for the shown reaction.
ΔG varies with reactant and product concentrations.
ΔG°′ alone does not determine cellular direction.

terms.meaning: Current product-to-reactant concentration ratio used before equilibrium.

interaction.q: Why can actual ΔG differ from ΔG°′?
options: Actual concentrations may differ from standard conditions
interaction.explanation: The RT ln concentration-ratio term makes actual ΔG depend on current concentrations.

title: Glycolysis as a reaction sequence
explain: The diagram presents glycolysis as linked enzyme-catalyzed steps converting glucose toward pyruvate, with ATP used in early steps and energy captured later as ATP and NADH.
mustKnow: Glycolysis is a multistep pathway.
ATP is consumed in early phosphorylation steps.
Later steps produce ATP and NADH.
The pathway proceeds from glucose toward pyruvate.

terms.meaning: Pathway that converts glucose through multiple steps toward pyruvate.
Reduced electron-carrying form of NAD+.
Addition or transfer of a phosphoryl group.

interaction.label: Glycolysis links ATP investment to later ATP and NADH production

title: Free-energy changes are additive
explain: For consecutive reactions A → B and B → C, the intermediate B cancels in the net equation. The overall free-energy change is the sum ΔG°′1 + ΔG°′2.
mustKnow: Free-energy changes of successive reactions add.
A shared intermediate cancels from the net reaction.
The net reaction shown is A → C.

terms.meaning: Molecule produced in one step and consumed in a later step.
Overall reaction after canceling shared intermediates.

interaction.q: If A → B has ΔG°′1 and B → C has ΔG°′2, the ΔG°′ for A → C is:
interaction.explanation: Standard free-energy changes are additive for consecutive reactions.

title: Coupling unfavorable and favorable reactions
explain: An unfavorable glucose phosphorylation can proceed when coupled to favorable ATP hydrolysis through a shared intermediate. Adding +13.8 and −30.5 kJ/mol gives a negative overall ΔG°′ of −16.7 kJ/mol.
mustKnow: Reaction coupling adds component ΔG values.
ATP hydrolysis can drive an endergonic reaction.
The shown coupled reaction has ΔG°′ = −16.7 kJ/mol.
A negative overall ΔG°′ makes the combined process favorable.

terms.meaning: Linking an unfavorable reaction to a favorable one so the combined ΔG is negative.
Phosphorylated glucose product in the shown coupled reaction.

interaction.q: Why does the combined phosphorylation reaction proceed favorably?
options: ATP hydrolysis makes the summed ΔG negative
Glucose phosphorylation alone has negative ΔG
interaction.explanation: Adding ATP hydrolysis to glucose phosphorylation gives an overall ΔG°′ of −16.7 kJ/mol.

title: Free-energy summary I
explain: ΔG is the net result of bonding stability, represented by enthalpy, and energy dispersal, represented by entropy. ΔG°′ is a reaction constant linked to equilibrium, while actual ΔG also includes current concentrations.
mustKnow: ΔG reflects both enthalpy and entropy.
ΔG°′ can be calculated from K′eq.
Actual ΔG depends on ΔG°′ and concentrations.

terms.meaning: Thermodynamic quantity associated here with bonding and heat.
Reaction-specific free-energy change under biochemical standard conditions.

interaction.q: Which quantity changes when cellular reactant and product concentrations change?
interaction.explanation: Actual ΔG contains a concentration-dependent term.

title: Free-energy summary II
explain: Negative ΔG favors forward reaction, positive ΔG favors reverse reaction, and ΔG = 0 marks equilibrium. ΔG does not depend on the route taken, and stepwise ΔG values add.
mustKnow: ΔG < 0 favors forward direction.
ΔG > 0 favors reverse direction.
ΔG = 0 at equilibrium.
ΔG is path-independent and additive.

terms.meaning: Depends only on initial and final states, not the reaction route.
State at which ΔG equals zero and there is no net driving force.

interaction.q: What is true when ΔG = 0?
options: The forward reaction is strongly favored
The reverse reaction is strongly favored
interaction.explanation: The slide states that ΔG equals zero at equilibrium.

title: ATP as the cellular energy currency
explain: ATP is the main energy currency used to drive metabolic and catabolic processes. Cells synthesize ATP, hydrolyze it to ADP and phosphate for work, and monitor the ATP-to-ADP balance as an energy-charge signal.
mustKnow: ATP is the main metabolic energy currency.
ATP hydrolysis produces ADP and inorganic phosphate.
The ATP/ADP ratio reports cellular energy status.
Low ATP relative to ADP promotes ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation.

terms.meaning: Adenosine triphosphate, the major cellular energy-transfer molecule.
Adenosine diphosphate, produced when ATP loses a phosphate.
Cellular energy status reflected by adenine nucleotide ratios.
Process that synthesizes ATP when cellular energy is low.

interaction.q: A cell with more ADP than ATP must primarily:
interaction.explanation: The slide states that when ADP exceeds ATP, the cell must synthesize ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.

title: Sources and uses of free energy
explain: Cells are isothermal systems that need a continuous free-energy source. Photosynthetic cells capture solar radiation, while heterotrophic cells obtain energy from nutrient molecules; both convert energy into ATP and other energy-rich compounds.
mustKnow: Cells require a source of free energy.
Photosynthetic cells obtain energy from sunlight.
Heterotrophic cells obtain energy from nutrients.
Cells convert captured energy into ATP and other energy-rich compounds.

terms.meaning: System operating at approximately constant temperature.
Cell that captures energy from solar radiation.
Cell that obtains energy from nutrient molecules.

interaction.q: Heterotrophic cells acquire free energy primarily from:
interaction.explanation: The slide contrasts nutrient-derived energy in heterotrophs with solar energy in photosynthetic cells.

title: Redox potential
explain: Redox potential measures a compound's tendency to give or receive electrons. The slide relates it to the ratio of reducing and oxidizing forms and notes the NAD+/NADH pair as important in bioenergetics.
mustKnow: Redox potential describes electron-donation or electron-acceptance tendency.
It depends on the ratio of reducing to oxidizing agent.
The NAD+/NADH ratio is metabolically important.

terms.meaning: Quantitative measure of tendency to donate or accept electrons.
Electron donor.
Electron acceptor.
Oxidized/reduced forms of a biological electron carrier.

interaction.q: Redox potential is a measure of a compound's tendency to:
interaction.explanation: The slide defines oxidation-reduction potential by electron-giving or electron-receiving tendency.

title: High-energy compounds
explain: High-energy compounds release substantial free energy on hydrolysis. The slide uses more than 7.0 kcal/mol as its cutoff and notes that many, but not all, contain phosphate groups.
mustKnow: High-energy compounds release more than 7.0 kcal/mol on hydrolysis by the slide's definition.
Low-energy compounds release less than 7.0 kcal/mol.
Many high-energy compounds are high-energy phosphates.
Not every high-energy compound must be a phosphate.

terms.meaning: Compound whose hydrolysis releases a large amount of free energy.
Bond cleavage involving water.
Phosphate-containing compound with high free energy of hydrolysis.

interaction.q: According to this slide, a compound releasing more than 7.0 kcal/mol on hydrolysis is classified as:
interaction.explanation: The slide sets 7.0 kcal/mol as the boundary between high- and low-energy compounds.

title: Classes of high-energy compounds
explain: The table groups high-energy molecules by bond type: acyl phosphates, enol phosphates, thiol esters, and guanidino phosphates. ATP and pyrophosphate appear among the acyl-phosphate examples.
mustKnow: Acyl phosphates include ATP and pyrophosphate in the table.
Phosphoenolpyruvate is an enol phosphate.
Acetyl-CoA is a thiol ester.
Phosphocreatine is a guanidino phosphate.

terms.meaning: High-energy class containing a carbonyl-linked phosphate arrangement.
High-energy phosphate class represented by phosphoenolpyruvate.
High-energy sulfur-containing ester represented by acetyl-CoA.
High-energy phosphate class represented by phosphocreatine.

interaction.q: Which compound is listed as a thiol ester?
interaction.explanation: The table places acetyl-CoA and acyl-CoA compounds in the thiol ester class.

title: ATP structure and cleavage
explain: ATP contains adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups. Removal of the terminal phosphate produces ADP + Pi, while pyrophosphate cleavage produces AMP + PPi; both reactions release energy.
mustKnow: ATP contains adenine, ribose, and three phosphates.
ATP → ADP + Pi removes one terminal phosphate.
ATP → AMP + PPi cleaves off pyrophosphate.
Both cleavage modes release energy.

terms.meaning: Inorganic phosphate.
Inorganic pyrophosphate, two linked phosphate units.
Adenosine monophosphate.

interaction.q: Pyrophosphate cleavage of ATP produces:
interaction.explanation: The slide shows ATP + H2O → AMP + PPi for pyrophosphate cleavage.

title: Standard versus cellular ATP hydrolysis
explain: ATP hydrolysis has ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions, but actual cellular ΔG differs because ATP, ADP, and Pi concentrations are unequal and far below 1 M.
mustKnow: Standard ATP-hydrolysis ΔG°′ is −30.5 kJ/mol.
Actual cellular ΔG is not the same as ΔG°′.
Cellular ATP, ADP, and Pi concentrations are unequal.
Cellular concentrations are much lower than the 1 M standard.

terms.meaning: Reference conditions used to define ΔG°′.
Free-energy change calculated with actual intracellular conditions.

interaction.q: Why is actual ATP-hydrolysis ΔG different in cells?
options: ATP has no phosphate in cells
Cellular ATP, ADP, and Pi concentrations are not standard
interaction.explanation: The slide emphasizes that intracellular concentrations differ from the equal 1 M standard state.

title: Mg2+ complexes with ATP and ADP
explain: In the cytosol, Mg2+ binds ATP and ADP. For most enzymatic phosphoryl transfers, the true substrate is MgATP2+, so the relevant standard free energy is for hydrolysis of the magnesium complex.
mustKnow: Cytosolic Mg2+ binds ATP and ADP.
MgATP2+ is the true substrate for most ATP-dependent phosphoryl transfers.
The relevant ΔG°′ is for MgATP2+ hydrolysis.

terms.meaning: Magnesium-bound ATP complex used by many enzymes.
Molecule that transfers a phosphoryl group to another molecule.

interaction.q: For most enzymes using ATP as a phosphoryl donor, the true substrate is:
interaction.explanation: The slide explicitly identifies MgATP2+ as the true substrate.

title: Actual ATP-hydrolysis energy in an erythrocyte
explain: Using erythrocyte ATP, ADP, and Pi concentrations in the ΔG equation gives approximately −51.82 kJ/mol, more negative than the standard −30.5 kJ/mol value.
mustKnow: The calculation uses actual ATP, ADP, and Pi concentrations.
The shown erythrocyte result is about −51.82 kJ/mol.
Cellular ATP hydrolysis can release more free energy than the standard value.

terms.meaning: Red blood cell.
RT ln term used to convert ΔG°′ to actual ΔG.

interaction.q: What approximate ΔG for ATP hydrolysis is calculated for the erythrocyte?
interaction.explanation: The calculation displayed on the slide ends at approximately −51.82 kJ/mol.

title: ATP use and production in glycolysis
explain: The pathway diagram marks ATP-consuming phosphorylation steps near the beginning and ATP-producing substrate-level phosphorylation steps later, alongside NADH formation.
mustKnow: Glycolysis first invests ATP.
Later glycolytic steps generate ATP.
NAD+ is reduced to NADH during glycolysis.
Energy transfer occurs across a sequence of intermediates.

terms.meaning: Direct formation of ATP by transfer of phosphate from a metabolic intermediate to ADP.
Molecule formed and consumed between glucose and pathway end products.

interaction.label: Track ATP use early and ATP/NADH production later

title: 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate transfers phosphate to ADP
explain: The diagram shows 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate donating a phosphate to ADP, forming ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate. Its hydrolysis is more favorable than ATP hydrolysis, enabling ATP formation.
mustKnow: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate has high phosphoryl-transfer potential.
It transfers phosphate to ADP.
The products shown are ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate.

terms.meaning: High-energy glycolytic intermediate that can phosphorylate ADP.
Tendency of a molecule to donate a phosphoryl group.

interaction.q: What does 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate produce when it transfers phosphate to ADP?
interaction.explanation: The reaction diagram shows phosphate transfer to ADP, yielding ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate.

title: Why phosphoenolpyruvate has high transfer potential
explain: Phosphoenolpyruvate hydrolysis first forms an enol form of pyruvate, which then rearranges to the more stable keto form. This product stabilization makes hydrolysis strongly favorable.
mustKnow: Phosphoenolpyruvate has high standard free energy of hydrolysis.
Hydrolysis forms enol pyruvate.
Enol pyruvate tautomerizes to stable keto pyruvate.
Product stabilization drives the reaction.

terms.meaning: High-energy glycolytic phosphate donor abbreviated PEP.
Rearrangement between structural forms, here enol and keto pyruvate.
More stable pyruvate form shown after rearrangement.

interaction.q: What helps make PEP hydrolysis strongly favorable?
options: Enol pyruvate rearranges to a stable keto form
interaction.explanation: The diagram highlights stabilization through enol-to-keto tautomerization of pyruvate.

title: ATP powers work through transfers and conformational cycles
explain: ATP commonly drives work by transferring chemical groups or by hydrolysis-linked changes in protein shape. These cycles power muscle motion and proteins moving along DNA, mRNA, or other tracks.
mustKnow: ATP energy is often delivered by group transfer, not isolated hydrolysis.
ATP hydrolysis can switch proteins between conformations.
Such switching powers mechanical motion.
Helicases, RecA, topoisomerases, and replication ATPases are listed examples.

terms.meaning: Three-dimensional shape adopted by a protein.
Enzyme or protein activity that hydrolyzes ATP.
ATP-dependent protein involved in separating nucleic-acid strands.

interaction.q: According to the slide, ATP hydrolysis can directly power motion by:
interaction.explanation: Hydrolysis-linked conformational cycling is described as producing mechanical motion.

title: Ranking phosphoryl-transfer potential
explain: The graph ranks phosphate compounds by standard free energy of hydrolysis. Compounds above ATP, such as phosphoenolpyruvate, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, and phosphocreatine, can donate phosphate to ADP; ATP can donate to compounds below it.
mustKnow: More negative hydrolysis ΔG°′ means higher phosphoryl-transfer potential.
PEP, 1,3-BPG, and phosphocreatine rank above ATP.
ATP occupies an intermediate transfer position.
Glucose 6-phosphate and glycerol phosphate rank below ATP.

terms.meaning: High-energy phosphate reserve capable of phosphorylating ADP.
Relative ability to donate a chemical group.

interaction.q: Which compound is shown above ATP in phosphoryl-transfer potential?
interaction.explanation: PEP is positioned well above ATP on the hydrolysis free-energy ranking.

title: Three group transfers from ATP
explain: ATP can transfer different groups depending on which phosphorus atom is attacked: phosphoryl transfer yields ADP, pyrophosphoryl transfer yields AMP, and adenylyl transfer yields pyrophosphate.
mustKnow: Phosphoryl transfer leaves ADP.
Pyrophosphoryl transfer leaves AMP.
Adenylyl transfer leaves PPi.
ATP is a donor of more than just terminal phosphate.

terms.meaning: Transfer of the terminal phosphate group from ATP.
Transfer of a two-phosphate group from ATP.
Transfer of the AMP portion of ATP.

interaction.q: Which ATP group-transfer mode produces PPi as the leaving product?
interaction.explanation: The diagram shows adenylyl transfer producing PPi.

title: ATP activates luciferin in fireflies
explain: Firefly light production begins when luciferase uses ATP to activate luciferin. ATP is cleaved to form luciferyl adenylate, converting chemical energy into a form used by the light-producing reaction.
mustKnow: Luciferin is the light-producing substrate.
Luciferase is the enzyme.
ATP activation forms luciferyl adenylate.
The pathway converts chemical energy into light energy.

terms.meaning: Firefly substrate that participates in light production.
Enzyme catalyzing firefly bioluminescence reactions.
ATP-activated luciferin intermediate.
Light production by a living organism.

interaction.q: Which molecule is the enzyme in firefly light production?
interaction.explanation: The slide identifies luciferase as the enzyme and luciferin as its substrate.

title: Oxidation produces firefly light
explain: With oxygen and luciferase, activated luciferin undergoes oxidative decarboxylation to oxyluciferin and emits light. Luciferase structure influences light color, and luciferin is later regenerated.
mustKnow: Molecular oxygen and luciferase are required in the shown light-producing step.
Luciferin is converted to oxyluciferin.
Light accompanies oxidative decarboxylation.
Species differences in luciferase structure affect light color.

terms.meaning: Oxidized product formed during firefly light emission.
Oxidation coupled to removal of a carboxyl group as carbon dioxide.

interaction.q: What accompanies conversion of luciferin to oxyluciferin?
interaction.explanation: The slide states that oxidative conversion to oxyluciferin is accompanied by light emission.

title: Gene Expression and Regulation
explain: This lecture follows information from genes to proteins and then examines how cells regulate that flow, especially through prokaryotic operons.
mustKnow: The lecture moves from genes and expression to operon-based regulation.

terms.meaning: Use of genetic information to produce a functional product.
Cluster of prokaryotic genes controlled together.

title: Lecture roadmap
explain: The lecture covers genes, replication, transcription, translation, positive and negative regulation, constitutive and inducible genes, and prokaryotic operons including the lac operon.
mustKnow: Expression topics include replication, transcription, and translation.
Regulation may be positive or negative.
Genes may be constitutive or inducible.
The lac operon is the main prokaryotic example.

terms.meaning: Gene expressed continuously under the stated conditions.
Gene whose expression can be switched on by an inducing signal.

interaction.label: Roadmap: gene → expression → regulation → lac operon

title: What is a gene?
explain: A gene is a segment of genetic material encoded in DNA. Genes pass between generations and contribute to inherited characteristics and disease risk.
mustKnow: A gene is a piece of genetic material encoded in DNA.
Genes are inherited from parents.
Genes contribute to characteristics and inherited disease.

terms.meaning: Segment of DNA carrying genetic information.
Passed genetically from parent to offspring.
DNA-containing structure that carries genes.

interaction.q: A gene is best described here as:
options: A piece of genetic material written in DNA
interaction.explanation: The slide defines a gene as a small piece of genetic material written in DNA.

title: Gene expression and the central dogma
explain: Gene expression is the multistep use of genetic information to produce proteins. The central dogma summarizes residue-by-residue information flow as DNA → RNA → protein.
mustKnow: Central information flow is DNA → RNA → protein.
DNA-to-DNA transfer occurs in replication.
DNA-to-RNA transfer occurs in transcription.
RNA-to-protein transfer occurs in translation.

terms.meaning: Framework describing information flow from DNA to RNA to protein.
Copying DNA into DNA.
Using DNA information to synthesize RNA.
Using mRNA information to synthesize protein.

interaction.q: Which sequence matches the central dogma shown?
interaction.explanation: The slide defines the central dogma as information flow from DNA to RNA and then protein.

title: DNA replication
explain: Replication duplicates DNA during S phase. It is semiconservative: each daughter DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
mustKnow: Replication is DNA synthesis or duplication.
Replication occurs in S phase.
Replication is semiconservative.
Each daughter DNA has one old and one new strand.

terms.meaning: Cell-cycle phase in which DNA is replicated.
Replication producing DNA molecules with one parental and one new strand.
New DNA molecule produced by replication.

interaction.q: Semiconservative replication produces each daughter DNA with:
options: One old and one new strand
One RNA and one protein strand
interaction.explanation: The defining feature is retention of one parental strand alongside one newly synthesized strand.

title: The replication fork
explain: At the fork, helicase opens DNA. The leading strand is synthesized continuously toward fork movement, while the lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments from RNA primers.
mustKnow: Helicase opens the parental DNA.
The leading strand is synthesized continuously.
The lagging strand forms Okazaki fragments.
RNA primers provide starts for DNA synthesis.

terms.meaning: Y-shaped region where parental DNA opens and is copied.
New strand synthesized continuously toward fork movement.
New strand synthesized discontinuously.
Short DNA segment made on the lagging strand.

interaction.q: Which feature belongs to the lagging strand?
interaction.explanation: The replication-fork diagram labels discontinuous Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.

title: Replication video references
explain: This slide contains external video links intended to reinforce the DNA-replication mechanism.
mustKnow: The referenced topic is DNA replication.

title: Transcription: DNA to RNA
explain: RNA polymerase converts DNA information into RNA. It binds a promoter, opens a transcription bubble, escapes the promoter, elongates RNA by complementary base addition, and terminates to release the RNA.
mustKnow: Transcription occurs in prokaryotic cytoplasm and the eukaryotic nucleus.
RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA.
The four listed stages are initiation, promoter escape, elongation, and termination.
Initiation begins at a promoter.

terms.meaning: Enzyme that synthesizes RNA from a DNA template.
DNA site where transcription machinery binds to begin transcription.
Locally opened DNA region being transcribed.
Stage in which complementary nucleotides lengthen the RNA chain.

interaction.q: Which enzyme carries out RNA synthesis during transcription?
interaction.explanation: The slide identifies RNA polymerase as the enzyme responsible for mRNA synthesis.

title: Template and coding DNA strands
explain: RNA is synthesized using the noncoding antisense strand as the template. The coding or sense strand matches the mRNA sequence except that DNA has thymine where RNA has uracil.
mustKnow: The antisense/noncoding strand is the transcription template.
The sense/coding strand has the same sequence as mRNA except T replaces U.
mRNA is complementary to the template strand.

terms.meaning: DNA strand read by RNA polymerase; also called antisense or noncoding.
DNA strand matching mRNA sequence except for T instead of U.
RNA base used in place of thymine.

interaction.q: Which DNA strand has the same base sequence as mRNA except T replaces U?
interaction.explanation: The coding or sense strand matches the mRNA sequence with thymine in place of uracil.

title: Eukaryotic RNA processing
explain: Eukaryotic mRNA is first made as pre-mRNA containing coding exons and noncoding introns. RNA processing removes introns by splicing and joins exons to create mature mRNA.
mustKnow: Eukaryotes initially produce pre-mRNA.
Exons are the coding segments shown.
Introns are noncoding segments.
Splicing removes introns to form mature mRNA.

terms.meaning: Initial eukaryotic RNA transcript before processing.
Coding segment retained in mature mRNA.
Noncoding segment removed during processing.
Removal of introns and joining of exons.

interaction.q: What is removed from pre-mRNA during splicing?
interaction.explanation: RNA processing removes noncoding introns and joins the coding exons.
